Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**ranginui** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Ranginui.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Ranginui" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Ranginui" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"ranginui" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Ranginui ‌place sky, ​fatherhood, creation ​at ​the center ​of ​a living ‌mythological world.

### ​Origins ​(Myth)

Ranginui ‌appears ​in polynesian ‌tradition as ​sky, ‌fatherhood, creation. ​The ​name's meaning, ​"'Great heaven' ​(Māori ​rangi 'sky, ‌heavens' ​+ nui ‌'great'), ​the sky ‌father prised ​apart ‌from the ​earth ‌mother Papatūānuku ​by their ​children.", ‌shapes the ‌narratives ‌told about ​this figure.

### ​Worship ‌and Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later tradition-keepers ​preserved ​Ranginui in ‌ritual, ​text, and ‌iconography, ​ensuring the ​name survived ​into ​the modern ‌scholarly ‌record.

The ​myths of ‌Ranginui ​survive in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ‌later retellings. ‌Each ‌version reflects ​the ‌interests of ​its tellers ​— ​poets, priests, ‌philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ​PuniCodex entry ‌does not ​privilege ​a single ​version; ‌it gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare them. ‌The restoration ‌Ranginui ​gives the ​figure ​a stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Ranginui ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Ranginui, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​sky ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Ranginui** (*ranginui*) ​— Sky, ‌Fatherhood, Creation ‌· 'Great ​heaven' (Māori rangi ​'sky, heavens' ​+ nui ​'great'), the ​sky father ‌prised apart from ​the earth ​mother Papatūānuku ‌by their ​children. — belongs ‌to the ​Polynesian tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under the domain ​"Sky, Fatherhood, ​Creation". The ​name means ‌"'Great heaven' (Māori ​rangi 'sky, ‌heavens' + ​nui 'great'), ‌the sky father ​prised apart ‌from the ​earth mother ‌Papatūānuku by ​their children."[^1].

**Ranginui** ​is the ‌sky father ‌of Māori ‌cosmogony — *rangi*, ​'sky', with ​*nui*, 'great'. ‌He and ​the earth ​mother Papatūānuku lay ‌locked in ​an embrace ​that left ‌the world in ​darkness, until ‌their children ​forced them ​apart so that ​light, and ​humanity, could ‌live between ‌them. He ​is separation and ‌longing: the ​rain is ​his tears, ‌the mist her ‌sighs, and ‌the space ‌between sky ​and earth ‌the world we ​inhabit.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Ranginui** and ​serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/ranginui/). ‌The displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description computed ‌from the ​displayed form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*ranginui* contains ​the same letters: ‌no recovered ‌diacritics or ​special encoding ​is claimed. ​The work here ​is consistent ‌citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌modern ​Polynesian orthographies; ​macron usage ​follows ​each tradition’s ​reference dictionaries. ‌Etymologically ​the name ​means "'Great ‌heaven' ​(Māori rangi ‌'sky, heavens' ​+ ‌nui 'great'), ​the sky ​father ​prised apart ​from the ​earth ‌mother Papatūānuku ​by ‌their children."[^1].

​The canonical ‌spelling ​**Ranginui** matches ‌the conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*ranginui* contains ‌the same ‌letters, ​so no ​lost diacritics ‌or ​encoding transition ​is claimed. ‌The ​editorial work ​is to ‌fix ​one reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ​provenance, and ​keep ‌the original ‌evidence visible. ​The ‌displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ‌computed from ‌the ‌displayed form ​itself.

meditation.body:
Ranginui is ​the god ‌of necessary ‌grief. The ​myth refuses ​the fantasy ​that love ​alone could ​sustain the ‌world: the ​parents' perfect ​embrace is ‌a prison ​for their ‌children, and ​the world begins ‌only when ​Tāne's legs ​force the ​lovers apart. ​What the ​story understands ‌— with ​a psychological ‌precision rare ​among cosmogonies ‌— is ​that separation ‌is not ​the failure of ‌love but ​its condition. ​Rangi and ‌Papa do ‌not stop ‌loving each ​other: the ​rain is ‌his tears, ​the mist ​her sighs, ‌and the ​whole weather ​of the ‌world is their ​continuing conversation.

‌To meditate ​on Ranginui ​is to ​meditate on ​every necessary ‌leaving — ‌the child ​who must ‌push away ​the parents ​in order ‌to stand ‌up, the ‌people who must ‌leave the ​homeland to ‌become themselves. ​The children ​win light ​and space, ‌but they ​inherit a ​wound, and ​the father's ‌grief falls ​on them ​daily as ​rain. The Māori ‌genius is ​to make ‌that wound ​sacred rather ‌than tragic: ​the tears ‌water the ‌flax, the ​mist feeds ​the morning, ​and the ​sky, for ‌all its ‌weeping, holds ​the stars.[^1]
